author: Shock Exchange
title: Intel Delivers - Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC)
text:
Intel CEO Brian Krzanich. Source: ibtimes.com
In 2016, Intel ( INTC ) announced a transformation from a PC company to one that "powers the cloud and billions of smart, connected computer devices." Growth businesses of the future - the cloud, data center, Internet of Things ("IoT"), memory and Altera's programmable semiconductors - would power the company. After its broken promises in the mobile sector, I was reticent to believe the company. Intel is slowing making me a believer.
Q1 2018 total revenue growth was in the high single digits. This was impressive for a company with $16 billion in scale. Revenue from the Data Center Group ("DCG") was up 24% Y/Y. Demand was broad based, and customers also showed an affinity for high-performance products that drove a higher ASP mix. Higher ASP equates to higher margins, which I will touch on later. The cloud segment also grew 45%, which is consistent with explosive growth experienced by Intel's cloud-based customer base.
The Client Computing Group ("CCG") grew revenue in the low single-digits. The segment continues to show traction, despite largely operating in a declining PC market. CCG still represents more than 50% of Intel's revenue. It throws off cash that can be used for buybacks or future acquisitions.
Total revenue from non-CCG segments grew by 15% Y/Y. In effect, Intel is delivering on its promise that non-CCG would drive the future. Of note, the company's Memory segment grew revenue by 20%. Its Optane chips are 1,000 faster than NAND - it could offer a compelling value proposition for customers looking for more speed but do not necessarily require the density of DRAM. Though not that big in terms of revenue, Memory could fuel future growth for Intel.
Operating Income Margins Are Melting Up The key to Intel's earnings growth appears to be an expansion of its operating income margins. Margins were 28% in Q1 2018, up from 25% in the year earlier period. The margin expansion amplified the impact of the company's revenue growth. Operating income margins for CCG actually fell 400 basis points, while margins for DCG were 50%, up from 35% in the year-earlier period.
The increase in ASP from sales of high-performance products was key. If DCG's business mix remains favorable, then operating income growth could continue to outstrip revenue growth.
The Apple Question Speaking of margins, Apple ( AAPL ) is still an important customer for Intel, Qualcomm ( QCOM ) and other vendors that sell into the PC or mobile devices. As Apple continues to add scale, it may need to improve gross margin if its top-line growth falters. Qualcomm is currently embroiled in a dispute over the level of its licensing fees, which has hurt Qualcomm's revenue.
Wells Fargo ( WFC ) analyst David Wong believes there's a real risk Apple could design custom chips for its iPhone X, cutting out Qualcomm or Intel. Captive parts specific to the iPhone could become a trend vis-a-vis chips sold on the open market. The growing sophistication of the iPhone could require captive parts or Apple may see them as a way to improve gross margin. Either scenario could hurt Intel's sales of chips into the mobile space.
Conclusion This was another strong quarter from Intel. With the stock trading at 26x earnings and the S&P just 5% below its 52-week high, I rate the stock a hold. It will likely trade in line with broader markets from here.
